title: The Computational Functions of the Inferior Olive: Clues From Evolution
abstract: Abstract Background Cerebellum-like structures, mainly studied in weakly electric fish, act to remove the effects of the fish’s own movements on the electrical signals they receive, but do not directly control movement, nor do they have a clear error signal. In contrast, the cerebellum does directly control movement – arguably the most prominent functional difference between the two structures. Anatomically, the most pronounced difference is that the cerebellum possesses an inferior olive. This conjunction suggests that the inferior olive carries out a function that is necessary for the control of movement. Summary This paper compares cerebellum-like structures with the cerebellum itself to examine how the evolution of the inferior olive conveyed the capacity for direct motor control. Cerebellum-like structures act as adaptive filters to remove self-generated sensory interference. However, issuing motor commands introduces a new problem, that of error. Because the output of a sensory-filtering circuit is an estimate of the sensory signal, it cannot serve as an error signal to calibrate movement. We review computational, behavioural, and evolutionary evidence showing that climbing fibres from the inferior olive supply this missing error signal. In short, the evolution of the inferior olive represents a marked expansion in cerebellar competencies, transforming a sensory cancellation device into a primary controller of movement. Key Messages The evolution of the inferior olive resolved the fundamental computational limitation of cerebellum-like sensory filters by providing a dedicated error signal, thereby enabling cerebellar participation in motor control and the learning of internal models. Empirical evidence across learning paradigms and evolutionary lineages supports the view that the primary computational function of the inferior olive is to supply the error signals required for this transformation in cerebellar function.
